questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Oracle's Bank Account Model organizes every account in a strict hierarchy — Bank → ________ → Bank Account.
questions.explain: Every bank account lives under a Bank Branch, and every Bank Branch lives under a Bank — one bank can have many branches, and one branch can have many accounts. This hierarchy is what lets Oracle keep every account a company uses in one place and grant access to it in a structured way.

questions.prompt: Harborview Metals Inc. is setting up a dedicated payroll disbursement account. The account needs to pay employees by EFT and also needs to show up correctly in reconciliation. Which bank account uses must be assigned to this account? (Select all that apply.)
options: Payables disbursement
Receivables receipt
Payroll
Cash Management
questions.explain: Payroll must be assigned so the account can be selected to pay employees, and Cash Management must be assigned because every account that participates in reconciliation and positioning needs that use, regardless of what else the account does. Payables disbursement and Receivables receipt cover paying suppliers and receiving customer payments — not what this account was set up for.

questions.prompt: An operating account has its Secure Bank Account by Users and Roles flag set to Yes. A user in the Payables Invoicing function — who has business-unit/function access to the account, but has never been individually named or granted a role on the account's Security tab — tries to select this account during payment processing. What happens?
options: The user can select the account, because business-unit/function access alone is always sufficient.

The user cannot select the account, because when Secure by Users and Roles is Yes, a user must be individually named or hold a named role on the account, and business-unit/function access alone is not enough.
The user can select the account, but only for Receivables transactions, not Payables.
The user cannot select the account, because the Cash Management Administration duty role was never granted.
questions.explain: Once Secure Bank Account by Users and Roles is set to Yes, the account's finest-grained security layer takes over: a user must either be named directly, or hold a role that's explicitly named, on that account's Security tab. Business-unit or function-level access — the middle security layer — stops being sufficient on its own once that flag is on.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly explains why some Oracle Fusion implementations route certain payments through a cash clearing account instead of posting them directly to the main cash GL account?
options: A clearing account absorbs the timing gap between when the GL records a payment and when the bank actually processes it, so the main cash account only reflects amounts the bank has confirmed.
A clearing account absorbs the timing gap between when the bank processes a payment and when the GL ever records it, so the main cash account only reflects amounts Payables has approved.
A clearing account is required by Oracle for every bank account before reconciliation can be enabled at all.
A clearing account replaces the need for a tolerance rule during automatic reconciliation.
A clearing account exists so that Payables and Receivables can share the same GL cash account without conflicting.
A clearing account is only used for accounts that are secured by named users and roles.
questions.distractorExplain: Option 2 is the closest wrong answer because it also names a 'timing gap' as the reason for a clearing account — but it gets the direction backwards. The real problem is that the GL records cash leaving today, when a check is issued, long before the bank actually processes it — not the reverse. The clearing account holds that amount until the bank confirms it cleared; there's no scenario in this course where the bank processes something before the GL has already recorded it.
questions.explain: A cash clearing account exists purely to solve a timing problem: Payables can record a reduction in cash in the GL the moment a check is issued, long before the bank actually processes it. If that amount posted straight to the main cash account, the account would almost never match the bank's own balance on any given day even though nothing was wrong. Routing it through a clearing account first, then moving it to the main cash account once the statement confirms it cleared, keeps the two balances meaningfully comparable.

questions.prompt: Match each bank statement format to the detail that correctly describes it.
right: Line-based format using numeric record-type codes (01, 02, 03, 16, 49...), the most common format for US bank statements
Line-based SWIFT message type organized into tagged fields like :20:, :61:, and :86:, used heavily outside the US
ISO 20022 XML format with nested elements, increasingly replacing MT940 in markets migrating to the newer standard
questions.explain: BAI2 is the US-centric, line-based format using numeric record-type codes. MT940 is the SWIFT message type using tagged fields like :20: and :61:, common outside the US. CAMT.053 is the ISO 20022 XML format positioned as MT940's long-term replacement in markets moving away from older SWIFT standards.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of getting a bank statement from the bank into a form Reconciliation can actually use, in the correct order.
items: The statement file arrives via automated SFTP delivery or manual upload into Oracle
The Load step reads the raw file and creates bank statement header and line records in a staging structure
The Import step validates the account mapping, checks for duplicates, and converts the staged data into real bank statement records
The statement's lines become available for reconciliation
questions.explain: A statement always moves in this order: it arrives (SFTP or manual upload), Load transcribes it into staging records without validating anything yet, Import validates and converts that staged data into real Cash Management records, and only after Import succeeds are the lines actually available for reconciliation.

questions.prompt: First Continental Bank upgrades its systems and starts sending ACH credits under transaction code 478 instead of the 475 code Harborview Metals Inc. has always mapped. Harborview's transaction code mapping table was never updated. What is the most likely effect on tonight's statement import and reconciliation?
options: The Import step will reject the entire statement file and no lines will load.

The statement will still import, but the affected ACH credit lines won't be confidently classified under Oracle's standard transaction type, and automatic reconciliation won't match them the way it matches properly mapped lines.
Oracle will automatically detect the new code and create the mapping on its own.
The affected lines will reconcile normally, since matching rules only look at amount and date, never the transaction code.
questions.explain: An unmapped transaction code is a setup gap, not a file-level error — the statement still imports, but a line with no configured mapping can't be confidently classified into one of Oracle's standard transaction types, so the matching rules that depend on that classification won't treat it the way they treat correctly mapped lines. The fix is to add the missing mapping once, not to manually fix each statement line.

questions.prompt: Per this course, which of the following bank statement problems typically trace back to a configuration/setup gap rather than a genuine one-time file problem? (Select all that apply.)
options: An unmapped account number because the Bank Account record was never created
An out-of-balance statement where the transaction lines don't sum to the stated opening and closing balances
An unmapped transaction code with no configured mapping
A currency mismatch between the statement and the bank account's defined currency
questions.explain: Unmapped account numbers, unmapped transaction codes, and currency mismatches are all setup gaps — something that was never configured — and the fix is to correct the setup once. An out-of-balance statement, by contrast, points to a corrupted file, a bank-side error, or a parsing problem, not a configuration gap in Oracle.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: inside a matching rule, a tolerance rule allowing a small variance in amount can only be associated with a match type of ________.
questions.explain: Tolerance only applies when the matching rule's match type is One to One. One to Many, Many to One, Many to Many, and Zero Amount rules don't support an associated tolerance rule — if a business needs that kind of forgiveness on a many-to-many scenario, it has to be handled another way, such as during manual reconciliation.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes when Automatic Reconciliation is the right fit for a bank account from when Manual Reconciliation should be the primary approach, per this course?
options: Automatic reconciliation suits high-volume accounts where well-tuned rules can clear most routine transactions; manual reconciliation suits low-volume accounts where building and maintaining rules isn't worth the effort.
Automatic reconciliation suits low-volume accounts where there isn't much to review; manual reconciliation suits high-volume accounts where a human needs to check every single line.
Automatic reconciliation replaces manual reconciliation entirely once it's configured, so no account should ever need manual review again.
Automatic reconciliation only works on payroll accounts; every other account type must be reconciled manually.
Manual reconciliation is a legacy feature Oracle keeps only for backward compatibility with older implementations.
The choice between automatic and manual reconciliation is based on the account's currency, not its transaction volume.
questions.distractorExplain: Option 2 is the closest wrong answer because it keeps the correct idea that volume drives the choice — but it swaps which approach goes with which volume. The course is explicit that automatic reconciliation fits high-volume accounts, so a well-tuned rule set can clear hundreds of routine transactions without anyone touching them, while manual reconciliation fits low-volume accounts where maintaining rules isn't worth the overhead. Swapping 'high' and 'low' is the one error here.
questions.explain: Automatic reconciliation is ideally suited to high-volume accounts, where configured rules can clear the overwhelming majority of routine transactions and free staff time for real exceptions. Manual reconciliation is ideally suited to low-volume accounts, where the overhead of building and maintaining matching rules isn't worth it — and manual reconciliation remains necessary on every account, high-volume or not, as the cleanup step for whatever automatic reconciliation leaves as exceptions.

questions.prompt: A check Harborview Metals Inc. issued appears to have already cleared on the bank statement three days before Payables voids it in Oracle. What should happen with reconciliation for this payment?
options: Nothing — a voided payment is automatically dropped from the statement by the bank.
The automatic matching rule will simply skip it, since voided payments are a recognized match type.
This needs manual investigation, since the statement and the system now disagree about what actually happened.
The system transaction should be deleted so it never appears in any report.
questions.explain: Voiding a check before it clears the bank is the simple case — there's no real bank event, so nothing needs to reconcile. But voiding a check that already appears to have cleared is a timing issue where the statement and the system briefly disagree about what happened, and that needs a human to investigate rather than an automatic rule to resolve.

questions.prompt: Harborview Metals Inc.'s month-end review turns up four unreconciled items: (A) a $1,200 check outstanding for 8 days, (B) a $600 Receivables receipt entered twice by a new AR clerk 11 days ago, (C) a $9,400 wire First Continental Bank applied to the wrong Harborview account 42 days ago, and (D) a customer payment visible on the statement that was never keyed into Receivables. Which of these require a correction made directly in a subledger (Payables/Receivables), rather than simply waiting or escalating to the bank? (Select all that apply.)
options: Item A — the outstanding check
Item B — the duplicate Receivables entry
Item C — the bank's misapplied wire
Item D — the receipt never entered in Receivables
questions.explain: Item B is a duplicate system entry, corrected by reversing the duplicate in Receivables. Item D is a missing transaction, resolved by recording it in Receivables. Item A is a normal timing difference (an outstanding check) that just needs to wait for the bank to catch up, and Item C is a bank error that has to be escalated directly to the bank, not fixed from inside Oracle.

questions.prompt: Match each reconciliation report to the question it's built to answer.
left: Cash to General Ledger Reconciliation report
right: What system-side transactions are open and eligible to match, but haven't matched a statement line yet?
Line by line, which statement lines reconciled, against what, and which remain unreconciled, for one specific statement?
Does the reconciled cash balance in Cash Management actually agree with the balance posted in the GL cash account?
questions.explain: The Transactions Available for Reconciliation report shows what's still waiting on the system side. The Bank Statement reconciliation report is the line-by-line working report for one statement. The Cash to General Ledger Reconciliation report compares the reconciled Cash Management balance against the GL cash account balance — the comparison month-end close depends on.

questions.prompt: At month-end, Harborview's Cash Manager runs the Cash to General Ledger Reconciliation report on the operating account and finds a $4,200 difference. The Transactions Available for Reconciliation report shows nothing obviously missing on the system side, and the Bank Statement reconciliation report shows all lines reconciled. What's the most likely explanation for the $4,200 gap?
options: First Continental Bank made an undetected error that needs to be escalated.
$4,200 in already-reconciled transactions simply haven't been through that day's Create Accounting run yet.
A statement line was duplicated during Load and needs to be removed.
A transaction code used on the statement was never mapped to an Oracle transaction type.
questions.explain: Since nothing is missing on the system side and every statement line is already reconciled, the remaining explanation is the one this course builds toward: reconciled transactions only become GL journal entries once Create Accounting runs, so a gap between Cash Management and the GL is normal and temporary whenever some reconciled activity hasn't gone through that process yet — it closes automatically on the next run.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: under the hood, a bank account transfer isn't a separate kind of object — it creates two ________ transactions, an outflow at the From account and an inflow at the To account.
questions.explain: A bank account transfer is built from two external transactions: an outflow recorded at the From account and an inflow recorded at the To account, linked by the same transfer reference. Everything that applies to external transactions — including needing to be reconciled before being accounted — applies to both sides of a transfer.

questions.prompt: During reconciliation, a Cash Manager creates a $35.00 external transaction directly from a bank statement line for a monthly maintenance fee that had no system counterpart. Before Create Accounting can generate a journal entry for it, what else needs to happen?
options: Nothing further for reconciliation — an external transaction created directly from a statement line is, by definition, already reconciled against that same line.
The transaction needs to go through a separate reconciliation step against next month's statement.
The transaction needs approval from the bank before it can be accounted.
The transaction needs to be re-entered in Payables as a formal invoice first.
questions.explain: External transactions must be reconciled before they can be accounted, but one created directly from a statement line during reconciliation is immediately reconciled to that same line at the moment of creation — there's no separate reconciliation step left to perform. It's ready for Create Accounting as soon as it's created.

questions.prompt: Harborview Metals Inc.'s US entity transfers funds to its UK subsidiary — a different legal entity — converting USD to GBP. Which of the following are true about this transfer, per this course? (Select all that apply.)
options: It requires intercompany accounting relationships to already be configured in the ledger
It creates two external transactions: an outflow at the US account and an inflow at the UK account
Cash Management itself calculates the resulting FX gain or loss when the transaction is entered
Each side of the transfer must be reconciled against its own bank statement before it can be accounted
questions.explain: Because the transfer crosses legal entities, it needs the intercompany accounting relationships already configured. Like every bank transfer, it creates two linked external transactions, and each one needs its own reconciliation before it can be accounted. The FX gain or loss, though, is calculated by Subledger Accounting during Create Accounting — not by Cash Management when the transaction is first entered.

questions.prompt: Treasury wants to know whether Thursday's scheduled payroll run will leave the operating account below its $100,000 minimum balance sometime this week. Which view should they check, and why?
options: Cash Forecasting, because it's designed to project several months out using historical trends.
Cash Positioning, because it's a short-horizon, account-by-account view built from the bank's reported balance plus reconciled and imminent near-term activity.
The Cash to General Ledger Reconciliation report, because it shows the account's current balance.
Cash Forecasting, because transaction-based forecasting always includes this week's payroll run by default.
questions.explain: This is exactly the kind of same-week, account-level question Cash Positioning is built for: a short-horizon view built from the bank's actual reported balance, reconciled transactions, and activity expected imminently, like a scheduled payroll run. Cash Forecasting looks further out and leans more on projection — useful for planning, but not the tool for a specific same-week balance question.

questions.prompt: Put Harborview's month-end cash-to-GL review in the correct order.
items: Run the Transactions Available for Reconciliation report to catch system-side items that should already have matched a statement
Work the Bank Statement reconciliation report's remaining unreconciled items by category
Run the Cash to General Ledger Reconciliation report to check whether Cash Management and the GL cash account agree
For any remaining gap, confirm whether it's explained by reconciled transactions that haven't been through Create Accounting yet
questions.explain: The workflow runs system-side first (what's open and should already be matched), then works the statement's own unreconciled lines, then checks whether Cash Management and the GL actually agree, and finally explains any remaining gap — most often reconciled activity that simply hasn't been through Create Accounting yet, which closes automatically once it runs.

questions.prompt: Harborview's automatic reconciliation match rate on the operating account drops from its usual 95%+ to under 10% overnight, even though the statement's Import step reported no errors. What should the Cash Manager investigate next, and why?
options: Whether the statement file was corrupted during delivery, since Import success doesn't rule out a bad file.
Whether the bank started sending a transaction code that isn't in the configured mapping, since an unmapped code prevents confident classification and blocks the matching rules that depend on it.
Whether the GL cash account was deleted, since that would stop all reconciliation.
Whether the account's minimum balance target was changed, since that affects whether reconciliation runs at all.
questions.explain: Import succeeding rules out account-mapping and duplicate-statement problems, so the next thing to check is a transaction-code mapping gap — a bank introducing or changing a code that was never mapped is exactly the kind of setup gap that silently prevents a large batch of otherwise-normal lines from reconciling, even though nothing about the file itself is wrong. The fix is to add the missing mapping once, not to touch each line.
